newsitem.title: USA: Death of bond plan for St. Paul agency expected.
newsitem.headline: Death of bond plan for St. Paul agency expected.

text.p: Municipal bond market participants said Monday that the St. Paul, Minn., Port Authority's announcement to stop trying to restructure about $250 million of revenue bonds to avoid a future default came as no surprise.

"It was obvious for two years (the authority) had no support from bondholders," said Darrick Hills, a vice president in research at Minneapolis-based Dain Bosworth Inc. "I don't think it will make that much difference in market trading."
John MacDonald, a senior vice president at Minneapolis-based Dougherty Dawkins Inc, agreed that no progress had been made on the restructuring.

He added that the death of the port authority's plan for its Resolution 876 Common Revenue Bond Fund bonds should not affect the agency's future trips to the bond market because any new bonds would not be issued through that resolution.

Neither firm reported any activity in the Resolution 876 bonds since Friday when the port authority announced it was unable to reach a consensus with the majority of bondholders on its third attempt to restructure the bonds.
Hills said retail bondholders who were not following the situation may try to get a bid for their bonds.

Last year, the port authority proposed repaying at least least 80 percent of the outstanding principal on the long-term bonds by issuing refunding bonds yielding about half of the original interest rate. Meanwhile, short-term debt under Resolution 876 would stay the same.
At that time, authority officials said approval of at least 80 percent of bondholders was needed to implement the plan.
Authority officials blamed the lack of consensus on "inherent financial conflicts" between long- and short-term and retail and institutional bondholders.

Authority President Kenneth Johnson said in a news release that the agency decided it could not continue to spend time or resources "on a restructuring effort that is not desired by a substantial majority of bondholders."

Anaysts at Standard & Poor's Corp., which rates the bonds triple-C, said Monday the rating reflects the absence of a viable work-out plan and the prospect of default on the bonds in June 2003. They added that no immediate change in the rating was expected.

The bonds are backed by repayments of real estate loans financed by the fund. A depressed real estate market in the 1980s imperiled lease payments on the bonds, leading the authority to start warning bondholders in 1991 that reserve funds securing the debt would be depleted prior to the bonds' maturity.
Last May, the port authority completed a voluntary tender of nearly $32 million of the bonds, which were purchased for $28 million.
